Vs.

full_judgment:
Md Joynul Abedin J: This Rule was issued at the instance of the complainant petitioner calling upon the Deputy Commissioner, Bagerhat to show cause why the order Nos. 9 and 10 dated 5-1-93 passed by the learned Senior Special Judge, Bagerhat in Special Case No. 2 of 1992 refusing to take cognisance in the absence of sanction shall not be set aside and why direction shall not be given on the Senior Special Judge to take cognisance of the offence as per law. 

 2. The short fact leading to the issuance of the present Rule is that, the complainant-petitioner filed a petition of complaint on 24-8-92 against accused-opposite parties Nos. 2 and 3 before the Senior Special Judge, Bagerhat under section 4 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 with a prayer for taking cognisance under sections 161 and 165A of the Penal Code alleging, inter alia, that the complainant is owner of a fish gher for shrimp culture and he invested Taka 5 lakh in that project of shrimp culture. Opposite Party No. 2 while attached to the Mongla police station as the officer-in-charge, asked the complainant-petitioner through accused opposite party No. 3, sub-Inspector of police also attached to the said police station, to pay an illegal gratification of Taka 50,000.00 and held out a threat that if he refused to do so he would create disturbance in various ways in running his fish gher. But the complainant-petitioner being a person of strong personality refused to concede to such illegal demand. The complainant-petitioner with a view to avoid harassment and interference in the running of his fish gher by the said accused opposite parties filed Title Suit No. 96 of 1992 with a prayer for injunction so that he may not be disturbed in the peaceful possession and running of the fish gher by the accused-opposite parties. At this the accused opposite parties became furious and again threatened the complainant-petitioner to implicate him in false criminal cases and also to harass him by arranging detention order against him. The complainant petitioner at this stage prayed for an anticipatory bail before the learned Sessions Judge, Bagerhat which was refused. The accused opposite parties however, expressed their desire not to disturb the complainant-petitioner in the running of his fish gher provided he withdrew the civil suit filed against them. In this background of the matter, the complainant petitioner decided to withdraw the civil suit but the accused opposite parties managed detention orders against the complainant petitioner. The complainant petitioner, therefore, moved the High Court Division and obtained release order in Writ Petition No. 1900 of 1992 and subsequently, obtained an ad-interim order of anticipatory bail in Criminal Misc. Case No. 334 of 1992 apprehending arrest by the accused opposite parties Nos. 2 and 3. In this background of continued harassment by the accused opposite parties in various manner the complainant petitioner filed the petition of complaint before the Special Judge, Bagerhat as stated above. 

 3. On receipt of the petition of complaint the learned Senior Special Judge examined the complainant petitioner on oath in terms of section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. But before taking cognisance the learned Special Judge vide order dated 24-8-92 sent the matter to the Additional District Magistrate, Bagerhat for judicial enquiry and report Thereafter, the Additional District Magistrate, Bagerhat enquired into the allegations, examined witnesses and submitted his enquiry report dated 7 -10-92 stating that the allegations complained of in the petition of complaint were true and genuine. The learned Senior Special Judge, thereafter, on receipt of the said report, asked for prior sanction from the Government vide his Crl. Memo No. 2163 dated 31-10-92 addressed to the Prime Minister's Secretariat (public Division) for taking cognisance for prosecuting the opposite party Nos. 2 and 3. But the government after having examined the matter refused to accord any sanction vide Memo dated 27-12-92of the Prime Mnister's Secretariat and this refusal was. accordingly communicated to the learned Special Judge. The learned Senior Special Judge thereafter by the impugned orders refused to take congnisance in the matter on the ground that there was no sanction from the government for prosecuting the accused opposite parties No. 2 and 3 in this case. The complainant petitioner thereafter filed the present criminal revision and obtained the Rule. 

 4. The learned Advocate Mr SK Atiar Rahman, appearing on behalf of the complainant petitioner, submits that although offences under sections 161 and 165A of the Penal Code are offences under the Criminal Law Amendment Act no sanction for prosecuting the accused opposite party Nos. 1 and 2, who are Inspector and Sub-Inspector of Police respectively, are necessary in terms of section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Because, according to him, the said police personnel are not liable to be removed by or with the sanction of the Government as they are not appointed by the Government but by the Inspector General of Police (IGP) nor they could be said to have allegedly demanded the illegal gratification while acting or purporting to act in discharge of their official duty. Mr Atiar Rahman, however, submits that the above requirements of section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are equally applicable in matters of government sanction under section 6(5) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act and since these are absent in the present case there was no necessity for the learned Senior Special Judge to ask the government for and obtain sanction. Hence, the learned Senior Special Judge committed illegality in refusing to prosecute the accused opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 on the ground of withholding sanction by the Government. 

 5. In support of his above contentions the learned Advocate of the accused petitioners relied on 3 cases, namely, the case of Md Ismail and another vs. Crown reported in 6 DLR 152, Rokeya Begum vs. Shafiqur Rahman reported in 2 BCR 1982(HCD) 4 and another case from the Indian jurisdiction namely, Niaz Muhammad Baksh vs. Emperor AlR 1939 (Sind) 148. 

 6. The learned Assistant Attorney-General, on the other hand, vehemently contends that since the alleged offence is an offence under the Criminal Law Amendment Act and the accused opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 are public servants as contemplated under description Nos. 7 and 8 read with Explanation-l to section 21 of the Penal Code, previous sanction of the government is a pre-condition to taking cognisance and holding trial of the accused opposite parties in term of section 6(5) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act. The learned Assistant Attorney- General submits that the requirements of section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are not applicable and cannot be read with section 6(5) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act. Since the cases cited above by the learned Advocate of the petitioner did not involve determination of the question of requirement of sanction under section 6(5) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act they have no manner of application in the present case. 

 7. Case of Md Ismail and another vs. Crown reported in 6 DLR 152 involved prosecution. of offences under sections 116 and 161 of the 'Penal Code, and a Division Bench of the High Court of the then East Pakistan relying on a decision of the Privy Council reported in 52 CWN 567 held, that in that case offering of bribe to a sub-inspector of police by the head clerk of the civil supplies department did not satisfy the requirements of section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and, as such, there was no necessity of obtaining any sanction for prosecuting the head clerk. Their Lordships while disposing of the case also observed that the sanction is also necessary for prosecuting a sub-inspector of police for demanding of bribe by such police officer inasmuch as such demand cannot be said to have been made in exercise of or in purporting to exercise his official duty. 

 8. The case of Rokeya Begum vs. Shqfiqur Rahman reported in 2 BCR 1982 page 4 involved the question whether protection given under section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was available in case of prosecution of a sub-inspector of police and police constables removable by the Inspector General of Police and Superintendent of Police respectively without sanction from the government In this case a Division Bench of this Court held that since the sub-inspector of police and the police constables were removable by the Inspector General of Police and superintendent of police respectively no sanction was necessary from the government under section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for prosecuting them. Since the offences alleged to have been committed by the said police personnel were not the offences of and triable under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, section 6(5) thereof dealing with the sanction for the prosecution of a public servant was not discussed. 

 9. The case of Niaz Muhammad Bakshrs, Emperor reported in AIR 1939 (Sind) 148 involved the question whether sanction was necessary from the government as contemplated under section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure while prosecuting a sub-inspector of police. In this .case a Division Bench of Sind High Court also held in the light of section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure that since an inspector of police was liable to be removed by the Inspector General as per section 3(1) of Bombay District Police Act no sanction was necessary for prosecuting such police officer. 

 11.For the purpose of proper appreciation as to whether previous sanction of the government is necessary in the present case it may be worthwhile to examine the provisions of section 6(5) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act alone which are set out as under: 

 Provided that in case where the complaint or report referred to in sub-section (1) of section 4 is not accompanied by such sanctions the Special Judge shall immediately on receipt of complaint or report address by letter the Government in the matter and if the required sanction is neither received nor refused within sixty days of the receipt of the letter by the Government such sanction shall be deemed to have been duly accorded. 

 Provided further that as such sanction shall be required in respect of a case transferred under sub-section (3) of section 4 or by virtue of sub-section (4) of section 5, if such sanction in respect thereof has been duly accorded or deemed to have been so accorded before the case is so transferred. " 

 13. Since the Government in this case withheld sanction the learned Senior Special Judge rightly passed the impugned order refusing to take cognisance against the accused opposite parties and proceed with the case. Since the cases cited above on behalf of the complainant petitioners as mentioned above do not involve trial of offence under the Criminal Law Amendment Act they do not help them as they have no manner of application in the present case.
